records.found: Nothing dated between 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-09 bears on this entry: no paper, registry change, company release or regulator decision on a drug that lengthens telomeres. One older fact is missing from the entry: the United States trial registry posted results on 2026-10-27 for the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute's low-dose danazol trial in telomere diseases (registry entry NCT03312400), which was stopped for poor enrolment after 18 people. The entry's estimate says the other danazol trials are 'small, completed or of unknown status' and does not mention this one or its posted results.

findings.what: The trial registry posted first results for the low-dose danazol trial in telomere diseases (registry entry NCT03312400; sponsor the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute). Status: terminated, 'Study was stopped due to poor accrual'; 18 people enrolled; primary completion 2025-10-31. The posted main result counts people whose rate of telomere shortening fell by at least half at six months: 5 of 8 on the lower dose and 5 of 10 on the higher dose (Fisher exact p = 0.664). The entry's own caveat says the early closure limited the trial's statistical power. No telomere-length figures and none of the secondary results are posted. No deaths are recorded.

A paper in PLoS Genetics on how common inherited faults in the telomerase gene (TERT) are in the general population and which illnesses go with them. It is about who has the faults, not about a treatment, and does not bear on the test.

records.found: On 2026-11-05 Intellia Therapeutics said, in its third-quarter release filed with the United States securities regulator, that it finished enrolling the late-stage nerve-disease trial of its transthyretin gene editor (MAGNITUDE-2) during the third quarter, with more than the 60 patients it aimed for; the trial registry changed that trial to 'active, not recruiting' with 67 enrolled on 2026-11-05 and still gives July 2027 for its main result. This pulls towards the early end of the range, because the estimate's earliest year (2028) rests on that trial supporting an approval first, and a fully enrolled trial with an unchanged date makes that path firmer; it does not change the likely year, because the larger heart trial is still enrolling (1,200 planned, main result estimated December 2027). No approval, no trial result and no new safety stop were reported in the window.

findings.what: Intellia Therapeutics' third-quarter 2026 release (exhibit 99.1 to a Form 8-K filed 2026-11-05): 'During the third quarter, the company completed enrollment in its MAGNITUDE-2 Phase 3 clinical trial in hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy (ATTRv-PN), exceeding its targeted randomization of 60 patients.' It also says the company 'has made significant progress advancing enrollment' in the heart trial (MAGNITUDE), and that during the third quarter it began giving trial doctors the immune-gene (HLA) genotyping results for patients enrolled or entering screening. The release gives no date for results of either trial and reports no new safety event.

Trial registry, MAGNITUDE-2 (NCT06672237): update posted 2026-11-05 (submitted 2026-11-04). Status now 'active, not recruiting'; enrolment 67 (actual); main result estimated July 2027, study end August 2028; no results posted. The site's records say only that enrolment had restarted.

Trial registry, MAGNITUDE heart trial (NCT06128629): update posted 2026-11-04 (submitted 2026-11-02). Status 'recruiting'; 1,200 planned; main result estimated December 2027, study end April 2028; 128 of 138 listed sites recruiting and 9 withdrawn; no results posted.

Intellia's quarterly report (Form 10-Q, filed 2026-11-05) repeats the account of the 2025 stop, the patient's death on 2025-11-05 and the HLA finding in the same terms the site already holds, and says the company is still engaging the regulator about that finding. It adds no new safety event.

Older fact, restated in the same release: in September 2026 the United States regulator accepted Intellia's licence application for its other in-body gene editor (lonvo-z, for hereditary angioedema, a disease of swelling attacks), gave it priority review with a decision date of 2027-03-10, and said it plans no advisory committee. The site's records hold only the company's earlier expectation that the application would be accepted in the second half of 2026. An approval in March 2027 would be the first of any in-body gene editor, but hereditary angioedema is not an age-related disease or a disease of DNA damage, so on a plain reading it would not meet this entry's clinic test; the author may want to say so in the notes before the date arrives.

CRISPR Therapeutics' third-quarter release (exhibit 99.1 to a Form 8-K filed 2026-11-02) says the United States regulator has granted its in-body gene editor for blood fats (CTX310, aimed at the ANGPTL3 gene) the Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation for two uses: severe high triglycerides and raised LDL cholesterol. The designation brings early meetings with the regulator and possible faster review; it is not an approval. The same release says early trials of two more in-body editors, for stubborn high blood pressure and for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, are under way.

CRISPR Therapeutics release, as listed in search results: early-trial (phase 1b) data for the same blood-fat gene editor in people with severe high triglycerides, presented at the American Heart Association meeting in Chicago, with a reported mean fall of 65 per cent in the target protein and 63 per cent in triglycerides. The page refused the reader (access denied) and no filed copy was on the securities regulator's site yet, so the figures are from the search summary only.

Paper in Nature (Mizoguchi and colleagues, 'In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering'): laboratory and animal work behind a second in-body editor for blood fats, with the fall in the target protein in monkeys lasting three years after one dose. The abstract says the results were the basis for a first trial in people that is under way; the paper reports no result in people. Abstract read on Europe PMC.

Editas Medicine's third-quarter release (exhibit 99.1 to a Form 8-K filed 2026-11-09): an Australian ethics committee has approved, and the Australian regulator's notification step is complete for, a first trial in people of its in-body gene editor for inherited high cholesterol (EDIT-401). The company says it expects to treat the first patient in 2026 and report first safety data in the first quarter of 2027. No person has been treated yet.

records.found: Nothing dated between 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-09 bears on this entry: no paper, registry entry or release reports a premature-ageing mutation corrected in a person, and no trial of such a treatment was registered. Two older facts are missing from the entry. On 2026-03-03 the Progeria Research Foundation announced a manufacturing agreement with Forge Biologics to produce its progeria gene-editing therapy, SamPro-2, with no date given for a filing or a trial. On 2026-09-24 a South Korean hospital registered a three-year study that only observes one child with progeria, to gather the comparison data for a future gene therapy that acts on RNA and not on the DNA letter itself.

findings.what: The Progeria Research Foundation announced that it 'has entered into a manufacturing agreement with Forge Biologics to produce SamPro-2', which it describes as its 'gene editing therapy designed to correct the single DNA letter misspelling that causes Progeria'. It calls the agreement 'a defining step toward Progeria gene therapy clinical trials' and gives no date for a filing with the regulator or a first trial. This suggests the first person would be treated in a planned trial that still needs its pre-trial studies, and not by the fast single-patient route the estimate's likely year (2029) assumes.

Trial registry entry NCT07839351, first posted 2026-09-24: Bundang CHA Hospital in Seongnam, South Korea, plans to follow one child with progeria for three years with no treatment, to build the record of the untreated disease 'for the Development of AAV-Cas13-Based RNA-Targeting Gene Therapy'. Status: not yet recruiting. It is an observation study, and the planned therapy would act on the RNA message, so it would not be a correction of the mutation as this entry's test asks.

Paper in the Journal of Clinical Investigation: a base editor carried by a single virus eased muscular dystrophy in mice carrying the human gene. Muscular dystrophy is not a premature-ageing or ageing-related disease, so it does not bear on the test; it is one more case of single-letter correction in a living animal. Title read, abstract not opened.

Preprint (Research Square, not peer reviewed) on the drug selinexor in skin cells from progeria patients, and a paper of 2026-11-06 in Pharmacological Research proposing two small RNAs for laboratory testing in progeria. Both are cell or computer work on treating the disease's effects, not on correcting the mutation. Titles read, not opened.
